content: Wheezing in infants and young children is a common condition, and its prevalence appears to be increasing, although the exact extent of this rise is uncertain. Most episodes of wheezing in this age group are triggered by respiratory viral infections. The treatment of wheezing in very young children remains a topic of debate, with anti-cholinergic medications frequently prescribed. However, clinical practices vary significantly, and the effectiveness of this treatment approach is still under scrutiny. The primary goal of this review was to evaluate the effects of anti-cholinergic therapy in managing wheezing in infants under the age of two years. This review represents the second update of the original analysis. To gather relevant data, researchers searched the Cochrane Airways Group Specialised Register of trials, reviewed reference lists of related articles, and contacted experts and industry sources. The search was last updated in June 2008. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared anti-cholinergic therapy with either placebo or beta2-agonists in children under two years of age who were experiencing wheezing. Children with acute bronchiolitis or chronic lung disease were excluded from the analysis. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility and quality of the included trials. Six trials involving a total of 321 infants across three different clinical settings were included in the review. When ipratropium bromide (an anti-cholinergic agent) was combined with a beta2-agonist, there was a reduced need for additional treatment compared to the use of a beta2-agonist alone. However, no significant differences were observed in treatment response, respiratory rate, or oxygen saturation improvement in the emergency department. Additionally, there was no significant difference in the length of hospital stay between infants treated with ipratropium bromide and those given a placebo, or between those treated with a combination of ipratropium bromide and beta2-agonist compared to beta2-agonist alone. Interestingly, when ipratropium bromide was combined with a beta2-agonist and compared to placebo, clinical scores showed significant improvement at 24 hours. Parents also reported a preference for ipratropium bromide over nebulized water or placebo for symptom relief when used at home. However, a subsequent search conducted in June 2005 did not identify any new studies to add to the analysis. In conclusion, the evidence does not strongly support the routine use of anti-cholinergic therapy for wheezing in infants. While some parents observed benefits when using this treatment at home, the overall data are insufficient to recommend its widespread, uncritical use.
